summary: Pointer arithmetic moves a pointer by whole elements, not bytes. The compiler multiplies by the pointed-to type's size, which is what makes array traversal with pointers work.

sections.heading: The scaling rule
sections.body: Adding `n` to a pointer advances it by `n * sizeof(*p)` bytes. For an `int *` at address 1000 with 4-byte ints, `p + 1` is 1004 and `p - 1` is 996.

sections.heading: Valid operations
bullets: Add or subtract an integer: `p + n`, `p - n`.
Subtract two pointers of the same type into the same array: gives the element count (type `ptrdiff_t`).

sections.heading: Invalid operations
bullets: Adding two pointers has no meaning and does not compile.
Arithmetic on `void *` (unknown element size; GCC allows it as an extension, standard C does not).

sections.heading: Walking an array
Subtracting pointers
sections.body: The result is a count of elements, not bytes.
Because addition is commutative, `i[a]` is even legal, though you should never write it. Indexing and pointer walking compile to the same machine code in most cases.
Forming a pointer is only defined within an array object or one element past its end. Dereferencing the one-past-end pointer, or going further, is undefined behavior even if it appears to work.
`unsigned char *` moves one byte at a time, so it is used to inspect raw object representation. Casting `int *` to `char *` lets you view each byte of an int.

subtopics.title: Pointers and 2D arrays
subtopics.summary: Row stride is part of the type.

sections.body: For `int m[3][4]`, `m + 1` skips a whole row (16 bytes) because its type is `int (*)[4]`. This is why multidimensional array parameters need the inner dimensions.

takeaways: Arithmetic is scaled by the element size.
Pointer minus pointer yields elements, not bytes.
Stay within an array (or one past its end).
